summary: We developed the SPHEREx Sky Blinker & Spectral Explorer, a public-facing interactive web tool designed to process and display near-infrared all-sky survey data from NASA's SPHEREx mission. The tool enables users to query any sky coordinates or benchmark targets, blink multi-epoch time-lapse images, perform epoch subtraction (En−E1) to reveal moving objects (such as brown dwarfs, comets, and asteroids) as distinct dipoles, and extract live 102-band near-infrared spectra (0.75–5.00 µm) highlighting key molecular absorption features (H2O, CH4 ,CO2). By bridging massive astronomical datasets with intuitive visual comparison and live NASA IRSA/Gaia integration, our tool empowers citizen scientists, students, and researchers worldwide to pitch in and make breakthrough astronomical discoveries.
details:
The SPHEREx Sky Blinker & Spectral Explorer is an advanced, production-ready astrophysics web application engineered to simulate, process, and visualize all-sky near-infrared spectrophotometric survey data from NASA's upcoming SPHEREx mission. Built as a fully self-contained, high-performance single-file application using HTML5,Tailwind CSS, and Vanilla JavaScript, the platform allows users to seamlessly navigate celestial coordinates, query live NASA IRSA TAP and Gaia DR3 astrometric archives, and interact with realistic multi-epoch survey cubes without installing heavy desktop software like DS9 or complex Python pipelines.


You can interact with the website to perform several core functions: to see a wider region of the sky, you can use the Field of View (FOV) buttons on the left sidebar (such as switching to 1°×1° or 2°×2°) or simply use your mouse scroll wheel directly over the canvas to zoom in and out smoothly, while panning across different sections of the star field is as easy as clicking and dragging your mouse anywhere across the main sky viewport. Using the top control toolbar, you can switch into Blink Time-Lapse mode and click the Play/Pause button to cycle through multi-epoch observations matching NASA’s survey cadence, which helps spot objects shifting position over time. Switching to Epoch Subtraction (En - E1) mode cancels out static background stars while revealing moving or variable targets—such as high-proper-motion stars, asteroids, or cold brown dwarfs—as distinct cyan-and-rose dipole residuals. Furthermore, clicking on any celestial source within the canvas targets it and instantly renders its full 0.75–5.00 µm spectral energy distribution (SED) on the right panel across 102 near-infrared bands, highlighting deep molecular absorption troughs like water ice, methane, and carbon dioxide.

Designed with rigorous attention to astrophysical realism, the tool incorporates accurate point spread functions, telescope diffraction spikes, annual parallax wobble, and zodiacal background noise models, alongside multi-mission catalog overlays and a citizen science discovery candidate logger with CSV export capabilities. By bridging massive space agency datasets with an intuitive mission-control interface, the project successfully lowers the barrier to entry for astronomical discovery, empowering students, educators, and backyard astronomers worldwide to participate in collaborative cosmic exploration and contribute directly to citizen science initiatives like Backyard Worlds.
